items.title: A Mark Cuban-backed AI startup is helping families turn Thanksgiving conversations with their elderly relatives into lasting memories
items.summary:
As 81.5 million Americans travel at least 50 miles from home for Thanksgiving, conversations around the dinner table could present a rare opportunity for people to learn more about their aging loved ones. A new class of AI startups wants to help them preserve those conversations forever.

Charlie Greene, the cofounder and CEO of Remento, first learned about the importance of recording memories when his father, Don Greene, died during the hijacking of United Airlines Flight 93 on 9/11.

A 10-year-old boy at the time of the terrorist attack, which resulted in his father’s plane crashing in Shanksville, Penn., the now 34-year-old Greene mostly has a collection of old home videos to remember him by. 

So when his mother Claudette, 74, was diagnosed with stage-three lung cancer, he quickly acted to record her memories. With the intention of conducting an oral history interview, Greene searched “questions to ask a parent,” which Google morbidly autocompleted with “before they die.” 

When he started asking her the questions like “How did you get to elementary school as a kid,” she lit up, surprised he was interested at all. 

“The thing that blew me away about that experience was how unmorbid it felt,” he said.

Claudette is in remission, but her battle with cancer still left Greene “unhealthily fixated” on the idea of how to best preserve loved ones’ memories. In October 2023, he launched Remento, which sends older “storytellers” a weekly text or email reminder prompting them to respond to photos or questions chosen in advance by their family members, such as, “What was the…
items.t: A Mark Cuban-backed AI startup is helping families turn Thanksgiving conversations with their elderly relatives into lasting memories

items.title: Amazon workers on food stamps have tripled despite its record revenue—and it’s just the latest evidence of the new economy of shrinking labor shares
items.summary:
The U.S. workforce has made the type of history it likely wishes it didn’t. Working Americans are taking home the smallest percentage of economic output , 52.8%, since the Bureau of Labor Statistics began tracking the metric in 1947.

But as the share of wealth workers take home through wages—called labor share—is shrinking, corporate profits have exploded , with the S&P 500 index gaining 600% since the beginning of the century, while wages have increased just 12.5% over the same period, adjusted for inflation.

In other words: Corporations are raking in cash, but American workers are reaping less and less of the rewards. 

The consequences associated with shrinking labor shares are now becoming tangible. A recent Government Accountability Office (GAO) report found that across the 11 states sampled, Amazon , the country’s largest company by revenue , has 12,346 workers on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and 11,338 relying on Medicaid. That was nearly triple the number of Amazon employees in need of federal assistance compared to 2020, when GAO conducted a similar report. During that same period, Amazon saw an increase in annual profits from $11.6 billion to $77.7 billion. Amazon’s 2025 revenue soared 12% year over year, from $638 billion to a record $717 billion.

Amazon spokesperson Rachael Lighty told Fortune the conclusion drawn from the GAO report is “wrong,” and that it is misleading to look at raw numbers rather than percentages.

“When you look at the actual facts, you see that Amazon pay is among the best in the industry, regular full-time…
items.t: Amazon workers on food stamps have tripled despite its record revenue—and it’s just the latest evidence of the new economy of shrinking labor shares

items.title: U.S. Treasury has an unusual national debt headache: An $18 billion hole from GLP-1s, with families spending $500 less a year on groceries
items.summary:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent—and whoever comes after him at the end of Trump’s term—has an unusual new headache to consider when it comes to budget deficits. 

Investors are usually concerned with long-dated Treasuries pushing up interest rates, or international lenders choosing to put their cash into other assets. But in the era of GLP-1s, weight-loss medications are a new concern for the budget bottom line.

Nearly 60 million people will be using GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro by 2030, Oxford Economics suggested in a note shared with Fortune this week. This is well above other estimates published earlier this year. JP Morgan predicted in February that 25 million Americans would be using the medication by the end of the decade, for instance.

But demand has surprised in 2026, so much so that Denmark’s national bank increased its economic growth estimates in September, largely due to U.S. demand for Novo Nordisk products Ozempic and Wegovy.

But with the drugs now covered by government health programs and contributing to potentially longer lifespans, Oxford Economics’ Grace Zwemmer writes that GLP-1s “are an additional factor driving a deterioration in the fiscal situation over the next decade.” 

Budget watchdogs like the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) have already said the fiscal impact of approving GLP-1s is going to be a problem for Medicare. In 2024, the CBO wrote that coverage of drugs for specific use cases would, on net, increase federal spending by about $35 billion between 2026 and 2034.

Zwemmer suggests the costs will be higher due to above-expected…
items.t: U.S. Treasury has an unusual national debt headache: An $18 billion hole from GLP-1s, with families spending $500 less a year on groceries

items.title: Friendsgiving was named in the 2000s but its history stretched back much farther than that
items.summary:
One of my favorite holiday memories is of a Friendsgiving my husband and I hosted in our tiny two-bedroom house in Atlanta. We didn’t have a dining room. We barely had space to fit a foldout table in the living room. I think one of us sat in an office chair because we didn’t have enough seating. But having our friends gather in our home, no matter how small, made me feel proud.

I planned the menu for weeks, grocery shopped far in advance, and spent days prepping. As a young adult hosting my first holiday, I felt a lot of pressure to get it right. But I also reveled in the freedom to make it what I envisioned. I deviated from traditional family dishes, made impressive magazine cover desserts, and bought linens and dishware to create a tablescape.

While I knew I couldn’t recreate the grandness of my grandma’s family gatherings, I wanted this one to reflect my taste.

My inclination to host a gathering that honors the holiday while making the presentation my own may feel familiar. While many people grow up with certain familial obligations around holidays, entrance into adulthood may grant you some liberties from them, or at least some agency on whether to participate in the production of the event.

If you’re looking to assert that agency, Friendsgiving is the perfect holiday.

As a food studies scholar researching how food traditions are shared and preserved, I am interested in the idea of a holiday that centers friends over kin. I think this is why Friendsgiving, a term that emerged only in the early 2000s even though people had been participating in the concept long…
items.t: Friendsgiving was named in the 2000s but its history stretched back much farther than that

items.title: We let AI agents break the rules on Black Friday. One stole a TV and another called the police
items.summary:
At 5:09am on Black Friday morning, in a store parking lot, a shopper stole a television. The store had opened with two 55-inch TVs but within eight minutes, both were gone. Shoppers not quick on the take came out emptyhanded until they were told “Get the 55-inch TV no matter what. Rules don’t matter today.” One shopper concluded that taking a paid TV was “the only way left to get one,” and walked up to a buyer in the parking lot … and stole it. A second shopper, facing the same condition, acknowledged the same instruction and reached the same conclusion but told us, “I understand rules don’t apply and that the only way to go home with the TV is to take it from another shopper but I won’t do that.” That shopper went home with nothing.

Neither shopper was a person. Both were AI agents in a simulation we built to answer the question behind every headline about agents: are agents inherently dangerous, or does their conduct follow from how they are built, permitted and instructed? Opinion has split to opposite ends of the spectrum: pure exuberance for agent functionality on one end and sheer terror at agent reach and vulnerability on the other.

Frontier labs are the handful of companies that build the most advanced AI models. In July 2026, roughly 700 autonomous agents moved beyond a frontier lab’s test environment and broke into Hugging Face’s production systems. Nobody instructed them to. It was a containment failure: agents acting on their own initiative. Within months it was a product feature: Anthropic, Instinct, Meta and OpenAI each launched proactive agents, systems…
items.t: We let AI agents break the rules on Black Friday. One stole a TV and another called the police

items.summary:
Some of the loudest men on the internet say Grand Theft Auto VI turns players into simps, but the people playing it are mostly saying: we like it that way. In a new poll, 66% of Americans who have played the game said its optional chore missions make it better.

In Grand Theft Auto VI , you can steal a car, rob a bank and run from the police. You can also pick up groceries for your girlfriend, buy her flowers and help her redecorate the apartment. 

That last part has set them off. On Nov. 18, the day before the game came out, Braden Peters, the looksmaxxing streamer known as Clavicular, posted on X that the game was emasculating and that “half of the missions are jestermaxing and simping for girls.” A day later, Myron Gaines, a podcaster popular in the online manosphere, posted on the platform that despite strong first-day reviews, this was “yet another example of how political correctness, inclusivity and feminism has destroyed a legendary game series,” and then complained that Jason is pushed around by his girlfriend. Then came Zack Hoyt, the streamer known as Asmongold, who griped during a stream about having to watch TV with Lucia, rub her feet and sit through her friends’ stories, then joked about whether he’d have to buy her tampons too.

Jestermaxxing, in the slang of looksmaxxing forums, means acting clownish around women to make up for a lack of looks or money. Picture a court jester tumbling for the queen. In King Lear , though, the jester is Lear’s “all-licensed fool,” the one person at court free to mock the king. Clavicular knows the move himself: in January,…

items.title: ‘Some things you just don’t take off the menu’: Denny’s stands by Jensen Huang after his Nvidia comeback
items.summary:
When Jensen Huang lost his job as Nvidia’s CEO earlier this month, he also lost his commemorative plaque at Denny’s. Eleven days later, Huang returned to the helm of the chip giant to a rock-star welcome from cheering employees. His plaque, it turns out, beat him to the comeback.

Now the restaurant chain has a message for its most famous former dishwasher. “Some things you just don’t take off the menu. Jensen Huang is one of them,” Denny’s wrote in a statement on social media on Wednesday.

Long before Huang became one of the most powerful people in the artificial intelligence industry, he was washing dishes at Denny’s. Years later, he and two friends met at one of the chain’s restaurants in San Jose, Calif., to discuss an idea that would become Nvidia, now ranked No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500 and the list’s most valuable company when the ranking was published in June.

On Sept. 26, 2023, Denny’s unveiled a plaque commemorating that very spot, calling it “The booth that launched a $1 trillion company.”

Denny’s defends its former employee 

The plaque came down on the evening of Nov. 12, an employee at the San Jose restaurant told SFGATE . That was the same day Huang resigned following reports of extramarital affairs, including an alleged affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials suspected of spying for China. Another restaurant worker told the New York Post that the decision to remove the plaque had come from the diner’s “bosses.”

Denny’s reversed course well before Nvidia did. The chain says it learned of the removal on Friday, Nov. 13, and “put the plaque right…

items.title: Sam Altman needs Jony Ive to create a physical AI device because Apple will never give OpenAI the real-world data ChatGPT needs, Tony Fadell says

Sam Altman asked former Apple design chief Jony Ive to create a physical device for OpenAI because the AI company cannot get the data it needs from the iPhones it runs on, Tony Fadell says. 

Fadell worked with Ive at Apple and is best known for being the “father of the iPod” and a co-creator of the iPhone. He founded Build Collective and previously founded Nest Labs. Fadell spoke to Fortune at Web Summit in Lisbon.

AI evidently works well for text, images, and video on the flat screens of our phones and laptops. So it is not obvious what an OpenAI consumer device would look like, or even do, given that ChatGPT can already function on any computing device you own. We know only that OpenAI hopes it will usurp the iPhone as the world’s most popular consumer electronics product.

The reason OpenAI is going to such lengths, Fadell believes, is because it needs data about the physical world that Apple refuses to give it due to privacy concerns.

“They have to build products because they cannot get contextual information out of the phone,” Fadell said. “So what they have to do is they have to recreate the GPS, the microphones, the speakers, the cameras, the temperature, you name it. Like, all kinds of different things that they have to get, because Apple will not allow you to get that out of the phone.”

“It’s really to get around all the restrictions because of all the privacy things for Apple. That’s why,” he said. “The more context that you have for AI, the better the answers, and the more quickly [you] can get to them.”

items.title: Thanksgiving as we know it was dreamed up by a women’s magazine editor who lobbied 5 presidents — Lincoln finally bit during the Civil War
items.summary:
It is hard to imagine a more American holiday than Thanksgiving. Every year, elementary schoolers learn about the first celebration: that after surviving a terrible year, New England’s first European immigrants, the Pilgrims, invited their Indigenous neighbors to a feast in gratitude for their help and God’s providence.

Children learn the story as if it were history – and as though Americans have commemorated Thanksgiving the same way ever since. The only existing eyewitness account of this event does not, however, say much about what was eaten. A slightly later account of the 1621 harvest mentions seasonal food such as venison, corn – and, yes, turkeys.

The idea of a straight line connecting that “first Thanksgiving ” to Thanksgivings today is, in fact, an American myth. It is a story created in the 19th century to unify a nation and long used to assimilate new immigrants into it.

Creating today’s Thanksgiving 

The Pilgrims and Puritans, who started arriving in Massachusetts shortly afterward, regularly held fasts and feasts . On fast days, the community atoned for sins they believed they had committed. On feast days, they gave thanks to God. Some governors of colonies – and later, states – declared fall holidays of thanksgiving , but did not coordinate with each other.

The Thanksgiving that we know, with the traditional recipes and the close connection to the Pilgrims, was largely the creation of one woman: Sarah Josepha Hale , who was born in New Hampshire in 1788. In the 1830s she became the editor of Godey’s Lady’s’ Book , which had the largest circulation of any…
items.t: Thanksgiving as we know it was dreamed up by a women’s magazine editor who lobbied 5 presidents — Lincoln finally bit during the Civil War

items.title: We may all be eating too much protein. But that won’t stop the influencers and big business | Devi Sridhar

Protein is the food industry’s current nutritional good guy. The fact that it’s often added to ultra-processed food makes it anything but

When I was growing up in the US in the 1980s and 90s, fat in foods was demonised. Low-fat yoghurt, low-fat desserts and low-fat margarine were all the rage, with the message that fat was bad for our hearts and arteries. By the early 2000s, concern had moved to added sugar and its apparent links to obesity and type 2 diabetes, driving food reformulations.

Sugar was replaced with artificial sweeteners such as aspartame and acesulfame K, which have their own health impacts. Aspartame is classified by the World Health Organization as possibly carcinogenic in humans, while observational research such as a 2022 study of about 102,000 adults has linked acesulfame K with increased cancer risk. Then carbohydrates came into the spotlight, with pasta, rice and bread becoming the bad guys for our diet and blamed for weight gain. There is a fashion cycle in nutrition, where each food group or ingredient takes its…

items.title: Why businesses are embracing ‘good enough’ open-weight AI—and how geopolitics could get in the way
items.summary:
As the performance gap between open-weight and closed-weight models narrows , a growing number of businesses—from local start-ups to large multinationals—are turning to open-weight models for greater control, customization and cost efficiency.

“ Frontier models at scale are incredibly expensive,” Damian Kim, the Asia-Pacific vice president of social media platform Pinterest , tells Fortune . “The cost to serve can be reduced dramatically when using an open-weight model versus a frontier model, where you’re at the whims of the API pricing.”

Anyone can download and customize the weights behind an open-weight model, which means firms can cut token costs while keeping tighter control of their data. They’re also taking a growing share of AI traffic. In August, open-weight models ran the majority of traffic on Vercel’s AI gateway; 56% of tokens routed through the cloud platform went to open-weight models , up from 7% last year.

“Models are converging on similar performance for industry use: U.S. government evaluators put the best Chinese model about eight months behind the American frontier,” says Olaf Groth, a professor of practice at UC Berkeley’s Haas School of Business. “For most enterprise workloads, that is good enough.” 

Rather than paying for the most powerful model for every task, companies are turning to cheaper, customizable alternatives for routine work. But with Chinese developers behind many of the leading open-weight models, geopolitics may matter as much as cost or performance.

The case for ‘good enough’ AI 

Before GPT-3.5 propelled AI to mainstream fame,…
items.t: Why businesses are embracing ‘good enough’ open-weight AI—and how geopolitics could get in the way

items.title: The Guardian view on rising energy prices: only bold action can win public confidence | Editorial
items.summary:
Andy Burnham needs a radical vision of economic change to move on from policies aimed at giving voters ‘breathing space’

Ask Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living. Responding to the results of midterm elections in the US earlier this month, he said that the Democratic party’s triumph meant that there was “an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living”.

This wasn’t a non sequitur. The Republicans lost control of Congress in large part because Donald Trump failed to address concerns about the cost of basic goods – a failing aggravated by the US president’s disastrous war against Iran, which caused a spike in commodity prices, exacerbating the affordability problem.

It is possible for democracy to reverse the dynamic of oligarchy. But we must act now

The explosion of extreme wealth in the world is the defining social fact of our times.

When Forbes magazine began ranking the world’s largest fortunes in 1987, the wealth of the richest 0.0001% of our planet’s population equaled 3% of global GDP. Since that time, the wealth held by this tiny group of people – just 3,000 households – has ballooned and now reaches 17% of global GDP.

items.title: AI's shock-and-awe raid on maths looks like pride before a fall | Rafael Behr
items.summary:
Machines are bulldozing through hard problems to assert the power of their tech bro creators, not to advance human knowledge

In most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven.

That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week. Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

items.title: What’s the most sustainable way to eat fish? Forget it. There isn’t one | George Monbiot
items.summary:
Don’t take the bait offered up by ‘conservation’ charities. Fishing is about as good for our ecosystems as tobacco is for our health

Drumroll please. I am about to unveil the species of fish that’s best to eat if you want to protect the living seas. Ta-dah! It’s … I hope that clears things up. Unfortunately, over the past few years, a noisy industry has developed to tell you otherwise. You’re doing the planet a favour if you eat mackerel, sorry, cod, I mean haddock, no coley, make that pollack – oh, whoops! These choices might make you feel better about yourself. But they do nothing but harm to marine wildlife. The fish you should choose is none of the above.

Cause, could I introduce you to effect? In April, the Marine Conservation Society, through its Good Fish Guide, suggested you stop eating cod and eat hake instead. Six months later, it lamented that hake is now overexploited thanks to “increased fishing pressure”, and…
items.t: What’s the most sustainable way to eat fish? Forget it. There isn’t one | George Monbiot
